I've been working this land in Quzhou for over forty years. I know the soil, I know the water situation — the aquifer here has been dropping since I was young, and that weighs on every decision I make. My education has helped me follow the research coming out of the experimental stations nearby. I read the provincial extension bulletins. I understand what's happening underground.

My land is about 10 mu. There's no question what I'll grow — winter wheat and summer maize, the same rotation I've always done, the same rotation my neighbors do. The wheat goes in around the 5th of October, comes out in June. Then immediately I put maize in on the stubble. Two crops, same ground, same year.

For wheat I'll use the Kenong 199 variety — it's drought-tolerant and does well in our soils. I'll do rotary tillage before planting to break up the compacted layer from the summer. I've cut back to three irrigations: winter water, jointing, and grain filling. The old-timers did five — I won't. The aquifer can't take it, and honestly the research backs me up on yield not suffering much.

For maize I'll direct-seed a hybrid, Zhengdan 958 or similar. No-tillage into the wheat stubble. I'll do two irrigations — one if summer rains are good, two if dry. Maize is more flexible than wheat.

Fertilizer I keep reasonable. I applied organic matter last autumn so I'll ease back slightly on nitrogen this cycle. Pesticide applications — two per crop, mostly herbicide and a fungicide pass on wheat.

At 63 my body reminds me not to over-extend. Ten mu is manageable alone with some family help at harvest.
